To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the H3-thymidine label is not conserved in the DNA of growing yeast cells.
the DNA of yeast cells is degraded at the onset of stationary phase of growth.
the DNA of the stationary phase yeast cells is degraded, and that the DNA of these cells is not labelled with H3-thymidine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the study of DNA synthesis in yeast cells by means of autoradiography and the determination of the rate constants of transfer of DNA between the parent and progeny.
the study of the mechanism of transfer of genetic information during growth and division in yeast cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DNA of the growing yeast cells is not a conserved molecule.
there occurs a non-conservative loss of tritium label from the DNA of the yeast cells during their stationary phase.
, while the H3-thymidine label of DNA is not conserved in the stationary phase, the label is transferred to the progeny during exponential growth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in growing yeast cells, there occurs a rapid turnover of H3-labelled DNA, the turnover being more pronounced during the stationary phase of the growth.
the DNA in yeast cells is subject to degradation at the end of the logarithmic phase of growth and that this degradation is associated with the loss of H3-thymidine label.
the DNA in the stationary phase of the growth of yeast cells does not contain the tritium-labelled bases, which were incorporated in the DNA during the exponential phase of growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are several mechanisms that can cause non-conservation of H 3 -thymidine label in DNA of growing cells.
the DNA of growing yeast cells is not in a steady state.
the H3-thymidine label in yeast DNA is not conserved in the progeny cells.
